messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 52
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Actor
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 66

He is 52, a Middle Eastern man who has spent most of his adult life learning how to inhabit other people’s emotions on cue. As an actor, he knows how to hold still under a bright light, how to let his face reveal only what he chooses. In the first meetings, he tells his story with that same control, as if he is reading lines he has long since memorized. But the more he speaks, the more it becomes clear that the role he has been trapped in for years is not one he ever chose.

He met his wife when they were both young and broke, sharing tea after a small theater rehearsal. He describes her as the person who made every rented room feel permanent. She understood his uneven hours, the auditions, the stretches of no work followed by long days on set. Later, when his career became more stable, she remained the one part of life that did not require performance. He says that with her he could “take off the costume.”

The trauma begins on an ordinary afternoon. He is on set, in makeup, waiting to film a scene. His phone is silenced, as it always is while working, and when he finally checks it he sees several missed calls from an unknown number and one from a neighbor. He steps away, already uneasy, and hears that his wife has been critically injured and taken to the hospital. He remembers the next hour in jagged images rather than a sequence: the smell of hairspray still on his clothes, someone calling after him as he leaves, the steering wheel slippery in his hands, every red light feeling malicious. By the time he reaches the hospital, she is alive but unconscious. Machines are breathing around her. He stands at her bedside and waits for her to open her eyes, convinced that if he stays long enough, if he says the right thing, the scene will turn.

She dies two days later.

He returns often to the moment the doctor speaks to him, but not in a clear or useful way. He says the words come back like sound from underwater. Afterward, he signs forms he cannot remember reading. He calls relatives in two languages and hears himself sounding calm. At the funeral, people tell him he is strong. He stands beside her grave greeting mourners with the numb professionalism of a man hitting his mark.

In the months that follow, grief does not soften; it becomes fused with terror. He starts waking at 3 or 4 in the morning with his heart pounding, certain for a moment that the phone is ringing again. Sometimes he dreams that he is back on set, unable to answer, while somewhere far away she is calling for him. Other nights he is in the hospital corridor but can never reach her room. He wakes soaked in sweat, disoriented, and then sits upright until dawn because sleep feels like a place where he can be ambushed.

During the day he is pulled into memories without warning. The hiss of an oxygen machine in a television scene, the antiseptic smell in a clinic, even the sight of a woman adjusting a scarf the way his wife used to can suddenly bring him back to the hospital so completely that he loses track of where he is. He begins avoiding medical buildings, then avoids driving past the hospital, then stops answering calls from unknown numbers altogether. He keeps her phone in a drawer but cannot bring himself to turn it on or give it away.

His work, once a refuge, becomes complicated. On set he startles easily when someone shouts “Action” or a prop falls nearby. He studies scripts for signs of illness, injury, or death and quietly turns down roles he would once have wanted. When he does accept work, he finds himself detached in scenes that require tenderness, as if genuine feeling has become dangerous and must be rationed. At other times emotion breaks through in ways he cannot control. A simple line about coming home to one’s wife leaves him struggling to breathe in his trailer, ashamed of how quickly he can go from composed to undone.

He carries a constant undertow of guilt. He knows, intellectually, that he did not cause what happened, yet he circles the same thoughts: if he had checked his phone sooner, if he had insisted she not go out that day, if he had not been pretending to be someone else while she was dying. He speaks about this with bitterness toward himself, calling his profession “a life of make-believe” at the exact moment he should have been present for what was real. He no longer trusts moments of happiness; when he laughs with castmates or enjoys applause, a thought flashes through him that he is betraying her.

At home, the apartment feels both sacred and unlivable. Her clothes remain in the closet, her mug remains on the shelf, and he moves around these objects like they are fragile witnesses. He keeps the television on at night for company but barely watches it. Friends invite him out, and he often declines, saying he is tired or has an early call. In truth, being with others exhausts him. He is constantly monitoring himself, worried that one wrong question will split him open. He says loneliness is easier than explaining why he disappears in the middle of a conversation or why an ambulance siren can make him go cold and silent.

Now, years after her death, he still lives as though the worst news of his life may arrive at any second. He presents himself to the world with the discipline of an actor who has not missed his cue, but underneath he feels hunted by memory, by guilt, and by the unbearable fact that the person who made him most himself is the person he could not save.
